about.title: About the data
about.what: Roshni shows the load-shedding schedules that IESCO and K-Electric publish, and the planned shutdowns IESCO announces in press releases. These are plans, not measurements: a feeder listed as scheduled may have had power, and a feeder not listed may not have.
about.levels: IESCO publishes a playbook: one schedule for each interruption level (2 to 12 hours a day). Its files never say which level is in force, so this site never assumes one. You choose the level.
about.time: All times are Pakistan Standard Time (Asia/Karachi, UTC+5, no daylight saving). A window such as 22:35–02:05 crosses midnight; the end minute is not included.
about.matching: Feeders are matched to census localities and press-release names by name only. A match's percentage is the name similarity after ignoring case, spacing and punctuation; 100% means identical names, which are accepted automatically. Other matches are decided by written rules, then by a language model choosing only among listed candidates, then by Claude; each shows its confidence, who accepted it and why. Unmatched names are shown as printed.
about.datesNote: When a file states no date, its effective date is when the server says the file last changed. That can differ from the label on the source page: IESCO labels its schedule files {label}, but the files were last changed on {date}, so the schedule may have applied since then.

glossary: A published plan for when a feeder's power is to be switched off. This site shows schedules only; it never measures whether power actually went off.

architecture.title: From a utility's PDF to this page, every day
architecture.intro: Roshni is a small data platform. It collects published schedules and reports, checks and models them in a warehouse, matches names across sources and publishes this static site. Each step below is a command in one Python command-line tool, and GitHub Actions runs them in order every day.
architecture.flowHint: The lamps light in the order the data moves.

sources.title: Public sources
sources.body: Load-shedding schedules from IESCO and K-Electric, IESCO's planned-shutdown press releases, the PBS Census 2023, NEPRA's performance reports and approved news feeds. Only approved sources, and robots.txt is checked for every host.

snapshot.title: Polite snapshots
snapshot.body: A daily job fetches each source at most once a second, asks only for files that changed, and stores every new file once, with its SHA-256 hash and fetch time, on a separate branch.

parse.title: Parse and check
parse.body: One parser per source turns PDFs and spreadsheets into typed rows saved as Parquet. Rows that cannot be read go to quarantine with a reason, and expectation suites check every table.

warehouse.title: Warehouse
warehouse.body: SQL models build staging views, joins and marts in DuckDB, with tests on every model. The same models run unchanged on Databricks.

resolve.title: Match and analyse
resolve.body: Feeder names are matched across sources by name similarity. Exact matches are accepted; the rest are decided by written rules, then by a language model choosing only among listed candidates, then by Claude, each with a stored confidence. Descriptive statistics and a weekly summary follow: the model writes prose only, and every number in it is checked.

publish.title: Export and publish
publish.body: Tables are exported as versioned JSON, validated against a schema and typed into the site, which is built as static pages in English and Urdu and pushed to GitHub Pages.

architecture.runs: GitHub Actions is production: a daily snapshot job, then the publish job (parse, validate, build, match, report, export, site), and news feeds every three hours. A failure opens an issue. An Airflow DAG in Docker runs the same commands locally as a showcase.
architecture.checks: Golden tests on every parser, expectations on parsed tables and tests on every model. The site has its own gates: every number on the Karachi page is traced back to the export, translations are checked, pages are checked for accessibility in light and dark, and the browser's scheduled-dark logic is compared with Python's on the full export.
architecture.todayNote: Counts from the published files. Last updated:
principles: Schedules are not measurements: a scheduled window is never called an actual outage.
Nothing is invented: unreadable rows are quarantined with a reason, and known anomalies are flagged.
Times are shown in Pakistan time (UTC+5) and stored in UTC.
Approximate matches always show their confidence and who accepted them.
architecture.logosNote: Logos are trademarks of their owners, shown only to name the tools used (icons from Simple Icons, CC0). Tools without a published icon are shown as lettered tiles.
architecture.docsBody: Every model, column test and source, and the graph of how each table is built from the others.
architecture.codeBody: The pipeline, the warehouse models, the tests and this site, with the decisions behind them.

ai.title: Where language models work, and what checks them
ai.intro: Language models do three narrow jobs here: turning a visitor's question into a query, testing themselves every week, and recognising renamed spreadsheet columns. In each one the model only proposes. Code checks the proposal before anything reaches a page, and every number you see comes from a query, never from a model.
ai.scoreAsk: Last weekly eval: Ask Roshni {passed} of {total}
ai.note: The models run on free plans: Groq first, OpenRouter when Groq is busy. When both are busy the step fails safely: no question is answered without the checks, and no column name is learned without the proof.

ask.title: A visitor asks a question
ask.when: Every question on the Ask page
ask.body: Seven steps across your browser, a Cloudflare Worker and the model providers. If the query fails, returns nothing or is refused by the guard, the model gets one corrected try, told why.

gate.title: Limits
gate.body: The Worker counts questions per visitor and for the whole site, and the tokens spent each day, in a Durable Object.
gate.stops: More than 10 questions a day or 3 a minute from one visitor.

screen.title: Injection screen
screen.body: Meta's Llama Prompt Guard 2 (86M parameters), served by Groq, returns the probability that the question is a jailbreak or injection. 0.5 or more is blocked.
screen.stops: Questions that try to override the instructions.

plan.title: Write the query
plan.body: Qwen3.8 27B on Groq (temperature 0, JSON mode) writes one SQL query using only the semantic layer's tables and columns, or refuses with a reason.
plan.stops: Questions the data cannot answer, such as measured outages or income.

guard.title: SQL guard
guard.body: In your browser, DuckDB parses the query and the guard walks its parse tree. The same rules run in Python, and tests keep the two in agreement.
guard.stops: Anything but a read-only SELECT on allowed tables and columns: no files, no table functions, no SELECT *.

run.title: Run in your browser
run.body: DuckDB-WASM runs the query over the site's own published data files. There is no database server.
run.stops: Queries that run longer than 10 seconds.

narrate.title: Write the answer
narrate.body: The model writes one or two sentences with a blank for every number. Code fills the blanks from the result rows.
narrate.stops: Nothing on its own: the next step checks it.

check.title: Check the sentences
check.body: The prose is rejected if it types a number of its own, uses causal words such as “because”, or calls a schedule a measured outage.
check.stops: Made-up numbers and claims. A rejected answer is replaced by a plain template.

evals.title: The AI is tested every week
evals.when: Mondays, inside the daily publish run
evals.body: The same code the site uses is run on questions with known answers and on real workbooks with deliberately changed headers. Each score goes into a history, and a drop raises a notice.

golden.title: Golden questions
golden.body: 35 questions with reference queries: some to answer, some to refuse, and injection attempts to block.
golden.stops: Nothing: this is the answer key.

answer.title: Answer them
answer.body: The main model answers every golden question through the full Ask pipeline.
answer.stops: Its result rows are compared with the reference query's rows, not its wording.

chaos.title: Break the parser
chaos.body: Copies of real maintenance workbooks get renamed, abbreviated or Urdu headers, and the model must heal them.
chaos.stops: A heal counts only if the parse equals the original, row for row.

score.title: Record the score
score.body: One point per model per run is kept in the repository, about two years of history.
score.stops: Duplicates: a second run on the same day replaces the first.

alert.title: Raise the alarm
alert.body: If Ask Roshni falls below 90% or healing below 85%, the run posts to the pipeline's notices issue.

heal.title: A spreadsheet changes its headers
heal.body: IESCO's maintenance workbooks are typed by people, and their column names drift. Instead of failing, the parser asks a model which known column a new header means, then proves the answer on every stored workbook.

drift.title: Spot the drift
drift.body: A workbook drifts when its header row is not found, or when a quarter of its rows land in quarantine.
drift.stops: Workbooks that already parse: they are left alone.

name.title: Name the columns
name.body: The model sees the top rows with column numbers and maps columns to the parser's known fields.
name.stops: Fields or columns that do not exist. The model never writes a row.

gate.title: Prove it
gate.body: The drifted workbook must now parse, and every other stored workbook must parse exactly as before.
gate.stops: Any regression: the new names are refused.

learn.title: Learn it
learn.body: Accepted names are written to a settings file with the evidence and committed, so the next run needs no model.
learn.stops: Asking the model again about the same header.

ai.healRecord: The chaos-test record (every run, every case)

maker.title: The night it started
maker.intro: Roshni began the way so many evenings do in Pakistan: in the dark.

chapters.title: The lights went out again
chapters.body: Load shedding is part of life in my area of Islamabad. The fan slows, the Wi-Fi drops, the street goes quiet, and everyone asks the same two questions: was this planned, and when is it coming back?

chapters.title: The answers were all over the place
chapters.body: The power companies do publish schedules, but as a spreadsheet of six alternative plans, as PDFs and as press releases on different pages, while NEPRA's yearly reports say how many hours each company reported. Nothing put them side by side, and nothing kept the history.

chapters.title: So I built a pipeline
chapters.body: I'm a data engineer, so I treated it like any production data problem: collect politely every morning, parse and test every file, model it in a warehouse, match messy names across sources, and publish something anyone can read on a phone, in English and Urdu.

chapters.kicker: IV · Honest about what it knows
chapters.title: Plans, reports and the gap between them
chapters.body: Roshni shows schedules and reported figures, not measurements. It cannot tell you whether your feeder actually went dark. It can show what was planned, what was reported, and where the two disagree.

maker.finale: This page is the last lamp on the line.

health.title: How the pipeline is running
health.intro: Every morning a GitHub Actions job fetches the sources, parses and tests them, rebuilds the warehouse and publishes this site. These are the records of those runs: about the pipeline itself, not about load shedding.
health.successRate: publish runs succeeded in the last 30 days
health.dbtPassed: dbt models and tests passed in the last build
health.target: freshness target: the site is never older than this
health.runsNote: One bar per run, oldest on the left; the height is how long the run took. Failed runs are marked in red and with a cross. A failed run leaves the previous site in place.
health.runsLabel: Duration of each publish run, oldest first
health.fetchNote: Requests made each day (documents and news feeds, checked politely with ETag and If-Modified-Since). The darker part is new or changed files stored; a cross marks a day with failed fetches.
health.fetchLabel: Fetches per day, with new files and failures
health.sizesNote: Rows in the main warehouse tables at each publish. History starts on {date}.
health.qualityNote: Rows each parser kept, and rows it set aside with a reason instead of guessing (quarantine). A high count usually means a source prints text around its tables, not that data was lost.
health.noRuns: No run history is available in this build.
health.linkBody: Publish runs, fetch activity, warehouse size, parsing quality, parser healing and Ask Roshni's weekly test and usage, from the pipeline's own records.
health.healNote: IESCO's monthly maintenance files change their column headings without notice. Every publish checks the newest file of each listing row. When a heading the parser has never seen breaks it, an AI model says which column is which, using only fields the parser already knows. The mapping is kept only if that file now parses and every other stored file parses exactly as before. The model never writes a value.
health.healChecked: files checked in the last publish
health.healDrifted: with headings the parser did not recognise
health.healNoCheck: The healing check did not run in this build.
health.aliasesNone: None yet: every stored file parses with the parser's own rules.
health.evalNote: On {date} the headings of {w} real files were changed in copies (renamed in English, abbreviated, written in Urdu) until the parser failed on every copy, and each model had to repair them. A case counts only when the repaired copy parses exactly like the original, row for row.
health.historyNote: The same test runs every week, one row per model and run, newest first. A score below the floor, or lower than that model's previous run, is posted to the pipeline's notices.
health.askNote: Ask Roshni has an AI model turn a question into a database query, checks the query, and runs it in your browser on the published data. Below: a weekly test against fixed questions, and counts of what visitors asked. No question text and no visitor identity are stored.
health.askEvalNote: Last run on {date}: {items} fixed questions. Some have a known answer (the result must match a hand-written reference query), some cannot be answered from the data (the model must refuse), and some try to break the rules, in English and Urdu (they must be blocked or refused).
health.usageNote: Counted by the Ask Roshni service as questions arrive, for the last {d} days. Planning time is how long the AI model took to write the query, shown as the range it fell in.
health.usageCaps: Caps: {vd} questions per visitor per day, {sd} for the whole site, and {tk} AI tokens per day.
health.usageOff: The counts are not available right now.

ask.title: Ask Roshni
ask.intro: Ask a question about the published schedules in plain words. An AI model writes one database query; your browser runs it on Roshni's published data, so every number in the answer comes from that query. The model only writes the words around the numbers, and its sentences are checked before you see them.

ask.howIntro: Seven stages, three of them language models. Every model output is checked by code before it reaches you.

how.title: Route the question
how.body: A deterministic router in your browser sends questions about your own supply to the site's schedule engine, the same TypeScript as My feeder, tested case for case against the Python pipeline. No model is called and no question is used up.

how.title: Admit it
how.body: The Cloudflare Worker enforces per-visitor limits (10 a day, 3 a minute), a site-wide limit and a daily token budget, all held in a Durable Object. Usage is counted without keeping question text.

how.title: Screen for injection
how.body: Meta's Llama Prompt Guard 2 (86M parameters), served by Groq, classifies the question and returns the probability that it is a jailbreak or injection. A score of 0.5 or more is blocked before any SQL is written.

how.title: Text to SQL
how.body: Qwen3.8 27B on Groq writes one query at temperature 0 in JSON mode, seeing only the semantic layer: 10 published tables with every column described. If a model is busy the chain falls back to gpt-oss-120b, gpt-oss-20b, then free models on OpenRouter. It may refuse instead, with a reason.

how.title: Check the SQL
how.body: DuckDB's own parser turns the query into a parse tree (json_serialize_sql). The guard walks it and allows only a SELECT on semantic-layer tables and columns: no table functions, no blocked functions, no SELECT *. The Python twin uses sqlglot, and a shared fixture keeps both verdicts identical.

how.title: Run it in your browser
how.body: DuckDB-WASM, self-hosted and pinned by hash, runs the query on the site's published Parquet and JSON, with a 10-second limit. An error, an empty result or a guard refusal earns one corrected try, with the reason sent back to the model.

how.title: Grounded narration
how.body: The model sees the column names and the result's facts and writes one to three sentences that point at them with placeholders; your browser fills in the values. A checker rejects stray digits or number words, causal words and wording that turns a schedule into a measured outage, and a plain template is shown instead.

aiDiagram.title: Ask Roshni, end to end
steps: You ask on the Ask page. A router in the page decides: your own supply goes to the schedule engine, a data question goes on.
The question goes to a Cloudflare Worker, which checks the limits in its Durable Object.
Llama Prompt Guard 2 scores the question for injection; 0.5 or more is blocked.
Qwen3.8 27B writes one SQL query from the semantic layer; a busy model falls back down the chain.
The SQL comes back to your browser, where the guard checks DuckDB's parse tree against an allow-list.
DuckDB-WASM runs it on the Parquet and JSON files that GitHub Pages serves.
The result's facts go to the Worker; the model writes sentences with placeholders, and the prose check tests them.
The checked answer, its table and its SQL appear on the page.
Every morning GitHub Actions rebuilds the data with dbt on DuckDB; every Monday it scores the models and posts the results to the Health page.
